gates.quick: ssh beast 'cd <worktree> && JOBQ_SUBMITTER=temper-cleanup ~/.local/bin/jobq submit --profile rust --project weir --cores 4 --mem 4G --timeout 3h --cwd "$(pwd -P)" --name <label>-quick -- bash .temper/gate-quick.sh', then `~/.local/bin/jobq wait <id>` until it ends (see the build rule)
gates.full: ssh beast 'cd <worktree> && JOBQ_SUBMITTER=temper-cleanup ~/.local/bin/jobq submit --profile rust --project weir --cores 4 --mem 8G --timeout 5h --cwd "$(pwd -P)" --name <label>-full -- bash .temper/gate-full.sh', then `~/.local/bin/jobq wait <id>` until it ends (see the build rule)

severity_notes:
- An acked `Durable` record that is not on disk, or does not replay after a crash, is severe. So is anything that lets two daemons own one `wab_dir`.
- A change to the on-disk WAB format, the wire protocol or a published crate's public API without a version decision is severe: it needs the owner (semver, the `docs_drift` guards).
- A panic reachable from a client frame, a stored segment or a config value is critical.
- A secret (sink URL credentials, bearer token, crates.io token) reaching a log, a `Debug` string, argv or `/status` is critical.
- Anything that loosens a security default (peer UID check, socket permissions, mTLS on TCP) is severe, and is never fixed overnight without the owner.

Scope of this epic (from its spec, docs/superpowers/temper/cleanup-2026-11/spec.md): the whole repository at the branch tip, NOT only `git diff main...epic/cleanup-2026-11` (the branch starts equal to main, so that diff is just the spec). Review the code itself, in your lens's area (the spec's Scope table). A finding needs an input and a wrong result that a verifier can reproduce; style, refactors and perf ideas are not findings.
These are owner items (kind owner), never fixes: a change to the WAB or `.confirmed` format, the wire protocol, `--json` shapes or a published crate's public API; loosening a security default; a new or upgraded dependency; D10 (explicit missing --config only WARNs: a deferred owner decision).
build_rule:
Every build, test, clippy or gate on beast runs as a jobq job: never run cargo, a gate script or a test binary directly in your ssh session (beast's ~/agents/CLAUDE.md; a session that compiled outside jobq was OOM-killed). Work in a worktree under ~/work/weir/ on beast; jobq's --cwd is that worktree's physical path (`pwd -P`).

Submit, then wait in the foreground (a single Bash call must stay under 10 minutes, so never use `jobq run` for a gate, and never end your turn while a job of yours is queued or running):
  ssh beast 'cd <worktree> && JOBQ_SUBMITTER=temper-cleanup ~/.local/bin/jobq submit --profile rust --project weir --cores 4 --mem 4G --timeout 3h --cwd "$(pwd -P)" --name <your-label>-quick -- bash .temper/gate-quick.sh'
  ssh beast '~/.local/bin/jobq wait <id>'   (call it again, with a Bash timeout of 600000 ms, until the job ends; its exit status is the gate's)
The full gate is the same with `--mem 8G --timeout 5h --name <your-label>-full -- bash .temper/gate-full.sh`. One cargo command (a reproduction, a single test) is the same with `--mem 4G --timeout 1h --name <your-label>-run -- bash .temper/gate-run.sh <cargo args>`, e.g. `... -- bash .temper/gate-run.sh test -p weir-wab segment`.
A job's env is cleared: pass variables as `-- env VAR=value bash .temper/gate-run.sh ...`. Read results from `~/.local/bin/jobq logs <id> --tail 400` (it prints only the last 200 lines by default) and from the gate's summary, /srv/bulk/Projects/weir/logs/gate/<worktree dir name>/latest-<quick|full|run>/summary.txt, whose last line is `GATE <name> rc=N`. A job's peak memory includes page cache: if a job is OOM-killed, resubmit once with a 2G larger --mem and say so in your result. Never cancel or touch another submitter's jobs. Keep at most one job of yours queued or running at a time. Beast's rule is at most 4 builds of this run at once: before each submit, run `ssh beast 'JOBQ_SUBMITTER=temper-cleanup ~/.local/bin/jobq list --mine | grep -cE " (queued|running) "'`; while it prints 4 or more, wait with `ssh beast 'sleep 120'` and check again.
Never set CARGO_TARGET_DIR or make another target dir: the gate slots are the build dirs; a gate that waits for a slot or for jobq's memory is normal. Never run sudo, never run the chaos harness's power-cut campaign, never touch docker images, volumes or containers that aren't weir's, never write the CI-skip token in a commit message. Commits carry only the `Temper-Task` trailer: no Co-Authored-By, Claude-Session or "Generated with" lines. Never print a secret or token.
A fix also adds one line under CHANGELOG.md `## [Unreleased]` (replace its "Nothing yet." line), in `### Fixed`, or `### Changed` for a behaviour an operator can notice, in the file's existing style. The `docs_drift` and `demo_drift` tests guard figures and version strings in the docs: if a fix trips one, fix the doc, never weaken the guard.
Clean up what you start on beast (test processes, tmux servers); leave worktrees in place.

selected.summary: In HTTP NDJSON batch mode the Idempotency-Key is the batch's content-only DedupToken, so distinct batches with identical bytes get the same key and an idempotent endpoint discards the later ones.
selected.input: sink_type=http, sink_http_batch="ndjson", sink_send_idempotency_key=true (the default), against an endpoint that honours Idempotency-Key (the reason weir sends it). Two separate batches with byte-identical record lists are sent, e.g. one-record heartbeat segments, or two 100-record batches of the same metering event.
selected.wrong_result: Both POSTs carry the same Idempotency-Key: sha256:<DedupToken>. The endpoint replays its cached 2xx for the second POST without ingesting it. The sink returns Ok, and the drain confirms and deletes the segment, so the second batch's acked records never reach the downstream. This is the same bug that per-record mode fixed in 2.0.2 by switching from a payload hash to RecordId, but at batch level. The S3 sink's key derivation (first RecordId + count + segment created_at) shows a replay-stable key that does not have this collision.

selected.summary: ClickHouse transport errors are formatted with reqwest's Display, which includes the full request URL and query string, without redaction. A password in the sink URL's query therefore reaches the WARN log, sink_failure/status and the health ERROR line.
selected.input: sink_url = "http://ch:8123/?user=default&password=s3cret" (ClickHouse's HTTP interface supports query-parameter auth). Then any connect or DNS failure, e.g. ClickHouse restarting.
selected.wrong_result: split_credentials strips only userinfo, so base_url keeps ?password=s3cret. reqwest 0.12.28 error.rs:268 appends " for url (<full url>)" to its Display, and commit() wraps it as format!("request: {e}") with no redact_url_password call. The drain logs it at WARN (drain/mod.rs, error = %e) on every retry and publishes it through ctx.publish.sink_failure. health() line 383 does the same, and drain/mod.rs:733 logs it at ERROR. The HTTP sink already redacts its transport error with redact_url_password, which scrubs password= query values, but the ClickHouse sink never calls it.

selected.summary: Preflight lets a producer socket whose parent directory is missing or not writable pass, so startup fails only at bind_all (main.rs:818). By then the drain has already been spawned with the replay backlog (main.rs:698) and is delivering. This breaks preflight's own contract that no refuse-to-start check may run after the drain has begun delivering.
selected.input: socket_path=/run/weir-x/weir.sock where /run/weir-x does not exist. This happens after a reboot clears tmpfs /run on a non-systemd run, or when the parent exists but the daemon user cannot write to it (connect gives ENOENT, so the probe reports Absent, but bind gives EACCES). The wab_dir holds a sealed, unconfirmed segment from an earlier run, the sink is reachable, and the daemon runs under Restart=on-failure (deploy/systemd/weir.service:86, RestartSec=5).
selected.wrong_result: Preflight passes. The test preflight_passes_when_the_socket_parent_is_missing asserts this on purpose. The daemon then runs recovery and scan_replay, spawns the flushers, and spawns the drain with the replay list, which starts committing to the sink. After the settle wait, bind_hardened fails (ENOENT/EACCES) and main returns Err (exit 1) while a sink commit is in flight. The segment is never confirmed, so each restart (every 5 s) re-delivers the head of the oldest unconfirmed segment and dies again. This is the unbounded duplicate delivery at the restart cadence that preflight.rs's module docs say preflight exists to prevent. Fix: preflight should check that the socket parent exists, is a directory, and is writable (e.g. open_parent_dirfd plus access(W_OK)) before recovery.

selected.summary: S3 classify() maps 400 AuthorizationHeaderMalformed, which S3/MinIO send for a wrong signing region, to Permanent, so a config error dead-letters the whole backlog.
selected.input: sink_type=s3 with the bucket outside us-east-1 and sink_s3_region left at its default us-east-1, or sink_s3_endpoint set to a MinIO/regional endpoint whose region differs from sink_s3_region.
selected.wrong_result: PutObject returns 400 AuthorizationHeaderMalformed ("the region 'us-east-1' is wrong; expecting 'eu-west-1'"). That code is in neither transient list, so classify(400, Some("AuthorizationHeaderMalformed")) falls through to `400 => Permanent`. Every batch is dead-lettered. health() reports HeadBucket's 400 only as Degraded, so the drain keeps going and the entire acked backlog ends up in the dead-letter log. The module's own rule (strand on connection-level rejection, as for SignatureDoesNotMatch, InvalidAccessKeyId and the config-header InvalidArgument) says this should strand.

selected.summary: The Postgres sink treats SQLSTATE 25006 read_only_sql_transaction as permanent and dead-letters every batch while the target is read-only, where MySQL's equivalent (1290) strands.
selected.input: sink_type=postgres when the sink URL's host is temporarily a hot standby (after a failover before DNS or the proxy moves), or the database has default_transaction_read_only = on during maintenance.
selected.wrong_result: Each INSERT fails with DbError 25006 "cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction". is_transient_sqlstate does not list it, so classify() returns permanent and insert_with_dup_fallback dead-letters the whole batch. While the condition lasts, every acked record drained is moved to dead letters instead of stranding and retrying. mysql.rs:356 classifies the same condition (1290, server in --read-only) as transient for this reason.

selected.summary: The MySQL sink treats server error 1040 "Too many connections" (and 1053 server shutdown) as permanent and dead-letters live batches on a transient server condition.
selected.input: sink_type=mysql while the server is at max_connections, so pool.get_conn() handshake gets ERR 1040, which mysql_async (conn/mod.rs handle_err) returns as Error::Server, the same path that makes 1045 a Server error. A second case is a MySQL restart that kills the in-flight INSERT with 1053 ER_SERVER_SHUTDOWN.
selected.wrong_result: classify() sends Error::Server through is_transient_server_code, which lists neither 1040 nor 1053 (nor 1203 max_user_connections), so the result is SqlSinkError::Permanent and the batch is dead-lettered. During a connection storm or a routine restart, acked records are moved to dead letters instead of being retried. The Postgres sink retries the same conditions: pool errors are always transient, and 57P01 admin_shutdown is transient.

selected.summary: attest verify reports a BROKEN_LINK (exit 1, tampering) when the drain deletes a segment out of order, which it does by design whenever an older segment is stranded, parked or quarantined.
selected.input: Shard with seg_00000001..3 sealed and attested (`attest seal`). The sink fails on seg_00000001 until its retries run out. The drain strands it, sets a not_before, and moves on (drain/mod.rs: 'held off until then while other segments move'). seg_00000002 drains, and confirm_and_delete removes seg_00000002.wab.sealed. The documented cron then runs `weir-ctl attest verify`. Reproduced on beast at 212f3e7: seal 3 segments, `rm shard_00/seg_00000002.wab.sealed`, then verify.
selected.wrong_result: `BROKEN_LINK shard_00/seg_00000003.wab.sealed expected_prev=a08e94... actual_prev=28bd09...`, `broken_links=1`, exit 1, and weir_attest_verify_failures>0, which fires WeirAttestVerifyFailed as an integrity incident. Nothing was tampered with. The design spec (2026-09-15 §3.2) and docs/monitoring.md say a segment whose predecessor is missing is reported as a chain origin, not a failure, and that 'a broken link always names a boundary between two segments that are both still on disk'. The walk treats the next surviving segment as the predecessor, so a gap left by normal out-of-order reclamation is reported as tampering. The predecessor's `.wab.confirmed` tombstone, which shows it was delivered, is never consulted.

selected.summary: attest shard_dirs treats every subdirectory except dead_letter/quarantine as a shard, so an unreadable lost+found makes `attest seal` chain nothing and `attest verify` exit 2 on every run.
selected.input: wab_dir on a dedicated ext4 mount, so it holds a root-owned 0700 `lost+found`. seal and verify run as the weir user, as in the documented cron and systemd units. Reproduced on beast at 212f3e7 with `wab/lost+found` set to mode 000 and a valid `shard_00/seg_00000001.wab.sealed`.
selected.wrong_result: `attest seal` prints `weir-ctl: read .../wab/lost+found: Permission denied`, exits 1, and writes no .attest sidecar. lost+found has no shard id, so sort_by_key puts it before every shard, and `sealed_segments_in(dir)?` (line 245) aborts the run. No shard is ever chained. `attest verify` prints `ERROR read .../lost+found: Permission denied ... errors=1` and exits 2 every run, so weir_attest_verify_failures stays above 0. This is separate from the known server-recovery lost+found finding: it is weir-ctl's own shard walk (shard_dirs). offline.rs/scan_segments share the same is_shard_dir_name filter.

selected.summary: attest verify and seal treat a sealed segment the live drain deleted after it was listed as an error (verify exit 2, seal aborts), unlike offline.rs, which skips NotFound.
selected.input: The documented setup: `attest verify --metrics-file ...` every 15 min and `attest seal` every 5 min against a running daemon's wab_dir. The drain confirms and deletes shard_00/seg_N.wab.sealed after list_segment_files returned it but before verify or seal opens it. Verify reads every segment in full, so this window is long when there is a backlog. The daemon never removes the segment's .attest, so the sidecar is still there.
selected.wrong_result: verify: verify_segment finds the sidecar, then SegmentReader::open fails NotFound. The `Err(e) => errors.push(...)` arm records `ERROR shard_00/seg_N...: No such file or directory`, exits 2 ('could not check'), and counts it in weir_attest_verify_failures, so WeirAttestVerifyFailed fires for a normally delivered segment. For a segment with no sidecar, chain_segment fails the same way at line ~679. seal: `chain_segment(&seg, prev)...?` (line 258) returns Err, so the run exits non-zero and leaves every later segment and shard unchained for that run. offline.rs already documents that a segment the live drain deletes between listing and open 'was delivered, so NotFound skips it silently'. attest does not.

selected.summary: push_batch checks each record against MAX_PAYLOAD_HARD_CAP but never checks the total frame body. The daemon caps the whole PushBatch payload at min(max_payload_bytes, 16 MiB), so a legal-looking batch goes out on the wire, gets Nack(PayloadTooLarge) back, and poisons the client. The method's doc says it guards locally against every Nack-and-close.
selected.input: WeirClient::push_batch(&[vec![7u8; 9 MiB], vec![7u8; 9 MiB]], Durability::Durable) against a default daemon (max_payload_bytes = 16 MiB). It also triggers with 2048 records of about 8.2 KiB each.
selected.wrong_result: The client sends a frame declaring payload_len 18,874,379 (more than 16,777,216). It gets Err(Nack(PayloadTooLarge)) with is_poisoned() = true and is_recoverable() = false, so the connection is lost. Expected: a local, recoverable rejection, as push() gives for an over-cap payload. Reproduced on beast with a throwaway test (jobq jq-01M6V945CJ05NHVXPWV5M99RSR), which printed: declared_payload_len=18874379 hard_cap=16777216 err=Nack(PayloadTooLarge) poisoned=true recoverable=false.

selected.summary: The docs say max_batch_records and max_payload_bytes multiply ('a batch of N records each up to max_payload_bytes is one frame'). The daemon actually caps the whole PushBatch frame payload at max_payload_bytes (connection.rs:207-209, before dispatch), so a batch can never be larger than one record's cap.
selected.input: Set max_payload_bytes = 1024 and send a PushBatch of 2 records of 600 bytes each. Each record is within the per-record cap the docs and the wire_protocol.md table describe.
selected.wrong_result: The daemon replies Nack(PayloadTooLarge) and closes the connection (connection.rs:209-225), but the docs say this batch is valid. Operators sizing memory from 'the two multiply' get the wrong worst case, and producers following the docs lose their connection.
